questions.question: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?
questions.title: Autoboxing and Unboxing
questions.direct_answer: Autoboxing is automatic conversion from primitive to wrapper object (int→Integer); unboxing is the reverse (Integer→int) — both happen automatically since Java 5.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's implicit type conversions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about NullPointerException from unboxing null, or == trap with cached Integer values
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention performance cost in tight loops and the NullPointerException trap

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Before Java 5, adding an int to an ArrayList meant writing Integer.valueOf(5) yourself. Getting it back meant calling .intValue() manually. Java 5 automated all of that.

content: Autoboxing: Java sees int where Integer is needed and silently calls Integer.valueOf() for you
Unboxing: Java sees Integer where int is needed and silently calls .intValue() for you
Both happen at the bytecode level — your source code stays clean

beats.content: Two traps to call out. First, NullPointerException: if an Integer is null and gets unboxed, Java calls null.intValue() and crashes. Second, performance: autoboxing creates real objects. In a tight loop over millions of numbers, you're creating millions of Integer objects — use int[] or IntStream instead.

sections.hook: Before Java 5 you boxed and unboxed primitives yourself. Java 5 made it automatic — but two traps hide inside that convenience.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So before Java 5, you had to manually convert between primitives and wrapper objects. Adding an int to an ArrayList meant writing `list.add(Integer.valueOf(5))`. Getting it back meant `int n = list.get(0).intValue()`. Tedious.

Java 5 introduced autoboxing and unboxing to handle this automatically. Autoboxing: when you put `int 5` where an `Integer` is expected (like ArrayList.add()), Java automatically calls `Integer.valueOf(5)`. Unboxing: when you use an `Integer` where an `int` is expected (like arithmetic), Java automatically calls `.intValue()`.

Two traps to know: First, NullPointerException. If an Integer variable is null and Java tries to unbox it (say you're doing int n = myInteger), you get a NullPointerException because it tries to call null.intValue(). Second, performance. Autoboxing creates objects. In a tight loop adding millions of ints to an ArrayList, you're creating millions of Integer objects. For that kind of work, use IntStream or a primitive array instead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Autoboxing: int→Integer automatically (Java 5+)
Unboxing: Integer→int automatically
NPE trap: unboxing null Integer throws NullPointerException
Performance: autoboxing creates objects — avoid in tight loops
Integer cache (-128 to 127) applies to autoboxed values too

questions.question: How can autoboxing cause a NullPointerException?
questions.title: Autoboxing NPE
questions.direct_answer: Unboxing a null wrapper object throws NullPointerException because Java tries to call .intValue() on null.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of subtle NPE causes beyond obvious null dereferences
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Being surprised that a line like `int n = map.get(key)` can NPE when the key is missing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete HashMap example which is the most common real-world occurrence

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The classic trap is a Map. You have Map<String, Integer> and write: int count = map.get("someKey"). If the key is missing, map.get() returns null. Java then tries to unbox that null Integer into an int — meaning it calls null.intValue() — and you get a NullPointerException.

content: The line looks innocent — no obvious null reference in sight
The NPE happens during unboxing, not during the map lookup itself
Fix: use map.getOrDefault(key, 0) to avoid the null entirely
Fix: assign to Integer first, check null, then unbox manually

beats.content: Same trap applies to any method that returns Integer — if it can return null and you assign it to int, you'll crash. Java 14+ helpful NPE messages do tell you exactly which variable was null, but prevention beats debugging.

sections.hook: One line — int count = map.get(key) — can NPE even though you never wrote null anywhere. Here's why.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So the classic scenario is a HashMap. Say you have a `Map<String, Integer>` and you do `int count = map.get("someKey")`. If the key doesn't exist, `map.get()` returns null. Java then tries to unbox that null Integer into an int by calling null.intValue() — and that throws a NullPointerException.

The fix is to always handle the null case: `Integer val = map.get(key); int count = (val != null) ? val : 0;` Or use `map.getOrDefault(key, 0)` which returns 0 if the key is missing.

Another scenario: a method returns `Integer` and you assign it to `int`. If the method returns null (which some APIs do to indicate 'not found'), the unboxing NPE happens.

The Java 14+ helpful NullPointerExceptions feature actually calls out exactly which variable was null, which makes these easier to debug. But better to prevent them with null checks or getOrDefault.

sections.title: Key Points
content: map.get() returns null for missing key
int n = map.get(key) → NPE if key missing (unboxing null)
Fix: map.getOrDefault(key, 0)
Fix: Integer val = map.get(key); if (val != null) ...
Ternary: int n = val != null ? val : 0

questions.question: How does autoboxing affect performance in loops?
questions.title: Autoboxing Performance
questions.direct_answer: Autoboxing in tight loops creates many short-lived wrapper objects, increasing GC pressure — use primitive arrays or streams instead of List<Integer> for performance-critical numeric work.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing that List<Integer> causes boxing for every add/get

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Every time you add an int to a List<Integer>, Java creates an Integer object on the heap. In a loop that runs a million times, that's a million objects — most of which become garbage almost immediately.

content: List<Integer>: every add and get triggers boxing or unboxing
Tight loop summing List<Integer> can be 3 to 5 times slower than summing int[]
IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream work with primitives internally — no wrapper objects created
int[] is the simplest fix for numeric accumulation

beats.content: That said, profile first. Most business code isn't in a hot loop over millions of numbers. Optimize when profiling shows boxing is the bottleneck — not before.

sections.hook: List<Integer> looks harmless. But in a tight loop it quietly creates millions of objects and hammers the garbage collector.

sections.title: Key Points
content: List<Integer> + int arithmetic = boxing for every operation
Tight loop summing List<Integer>: can be 3-5x slower than int[]
Solution: use int[] or IntStream for numeric accumulation
IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream are unboxed — no wrapper objects
Measure first: premature optimization; only optimize if profiling shows it

questions.question: What is the Integer cache in Java and why does it cause == comparison bugs?
questions.title: Integer Cache (-128 to 127)
questions.direct_answer: Java caches Integer objects for -128 to 127 — valueOf() returns the same object for cached values, making == return true for small ints but false for larger ones.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Comparing Integer objects with == and being surprised it works for 100 but fails for 200
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the JVM optimization motivation and confirm: always use .equals() for Integer comparison

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The JVM pre-creates Integer objects for values -128 to 127 and reuses them. When you autobox an int in that range, Integer.valueOf() returns the same cached object every time. Outside that range it creates a new object.

rows: Both point to same cached object

beats.content: The cache exists because small integers — loop counters, small indices — appear constantly in real code. Reusing objects saves millions of allocations. The fix is simple: always use .equals() to compare Integer objects. Never use == on wrapper types.

sections.hook: Integer a = 100, b = 100 — does a == b return true? It depends on the number. That inconsistency trips up engineers every day.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So the Integer cache is a JVM optimization where Integer.valueOf() reuses the same objects for values -128 to 127. Autoboxing uses valueOf() internally.

The trap:
```java
Integer a = 100, b = 100;
System.out.println(a == b);  // true — same cached object

Integer x = 200, y = 200;
System.out.println(x == y);  // false — outside cache range

System.out.println(x.equals(y));  // always true
```

Why -128 to 127? These are the most commonly used int values (loop counters, small indices), so caching saves millions of allocations.

Fix: ALWAYS use .equals() to compare Integer objects. Never use ==.
